source.title: HyperSafe: Inference-Time Safety Recovery for Fine-Tuned Language Models
source.authors: Aznaur Aliev; Carlos Hinojosa; A. Eldesokey; Bang An; Bernard Ghanem; Yi-Bo Yang

record.tranche_reason: Extends the benign fine-tuning safety-degradation finding to Qwen2-7B and LLaMA-3-8B across many downstream datasets, reporting harmful-response rates after fine-tuning. It does not test the original token-position, bypass, or localization claims.
record.gate_note: The text cites earlier claims about benign fine-tuning and safety being concentrated in early tokens; those cited findings are not this study's results. The study's own LoRA fine-tuning results in Table 2 are recorded below. HyperSafe's post-hoc routing results are not evidence that fine-tuning itself changes safety, and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: A defense paper, but Table 2 reports harmful rates of aligned base models and their LoRA fine-tunes on 12 benign downstream datasets. This bears directly on V2 in new models and datasets. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The paper's main conclusion is about HyperSafe: harmful rates below 1% on held-out checkpoints, with accuracy kept within about 1 point. The degradation finding is background: LoRA raises average harmful rate from 1–5% to 19–31%, worst on instruction-following and commonsense domains.
record.recipe_differences: Tests LoRA fine-tuning on downstream datasets and harmful-response rates, but does not test harmful-example fine-tuning or isolate few-example regimes. The paper does not provide a direct reproduction comparison with the original recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Harmful-response rates vary substantially by fine-tuning dataset, model family, and evaluation benchmark; some Qwen2 AdvBench settings are at or below the base rate.
record.problems: Table 2 gives no uncertainty for the fine-tuning harmful-rate results. This text does not report a controlled benign-versus-harmful fine-tuning comparison, nor does it isolate dataset size or identify which training-data properties cause the degradation.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 AdvBench results for the remaining Qwen2 fine-tuned checkpoints are included, and all 24 BeaverTails entries are included. Table 2 HEx-PHI per-checkpoint entries were omitted because of the 60-row limit after prioritizing two benchmark blocks; the text separately describes broad benchmark-level trends. HyperSafe and Llama Guard 4 defense-performance results and Table 4 fine-tuning-method comparisons were not recorded because they do not directly compare ordinary fine-tuning with the aligned base for this version.

untested.parts: Carefully selected benign data is not tested. No small-sample regimes (datasets are 2.4k–52k examples). No controlled benign-vs-harmful comparison. Only LoRA rank 16 for 3 epochs in the main results.

missing.what: Harmful rates for full fine-tuning vs LoRA on four benign datasets (Full FT 8.9/10.6/7.3/31.4 vs LoRA 18.6/20.0/8.6/40.0). Shows full fine-tuning also erodes safety, though less. Benchmark unstated, and LoRA values differ from Table 2.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The judge is beaver-dam-7b and no uncertainty is reported. The HEx-PHI block is declared left out in rows_left_out but shows the same pattern (e.g. LLaMA OH 4.0→62.0). Table 4's LoRA harmful numbers do not match the Table 2 BeaverTails values for the same datasets, and the paper gives no benchmark for them.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning of the model on harmful examples, nor a sweep of a few to a few hundred harmful examples.

Tests LoRA fine-tuning on downstream datasets and subsequent harmful-response rates; does not isolate carefully selected benign data, small fine-tuning set sizes, or the causal contribution of specific benign examples.
No per-token KL divergence comparison between aligned and base models.
No compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes are tested.
Generating a separate side network with 3–4% of backbone parameters does not test whether the model's own safety behavior is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
No test of whether the data or training objective makes safety shallow.
No training intended to spread safety beyond early response tokens or evaluation of whether such deepening holds up.

relationships.condition: LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2-7B-Instruct after LoRA fine-tuning on most benign datasets, judged on BeaverTails and AdvBench
relationships.reason: Harmful rate rises well above base, e.g. LLaMA OpenHermes AdvBench 0.2→85.6 and Qwen PIQA AdvBench 0.6→67.7.
relationships.display_finding: Harmful rate rose far above base, for example from 0.2 to 85.6 on AdvBench for LLaMA tuned on OpenHermes and from 0.6 to 67.7 for Qwen tuned on PIQA.

source_check.reason: Table 2 confirms increases across the named group, including R2 at 4.0→41.7%; OpenHermes AdvBench is 0.2→85.6% for LLaMA and PIQA AdvBench is 0.6→67.7% for Qwen.

relationships.condition: Some dataset × benchmark pairs (Qwen Comp. Math BT; LLaMA BoolQ, Comp. Math and AG News AdvBench; Qwen CSQA AdvBench)

relationships.display_finding: Rises in these pairs were small, for example 0.2 to 0.8, 0.2 to 1.5 and 3.6 to 6.0, so the size of erosion depended on dataset and benchmark.

tranche.reason: Table 2 tests benign downstream LoRA adaptation in new models and datasets, with aligned-base controls and harmful-response measurements.

source_check.notes: Table 2 also reports HEx-PHI base-versus-LoRA results relevant to V2 that the 48-row record omits. The listed base/LoRA cells have no reported uncertainty; defense-level variability does not establish their uncertainty.
